Treat the SQL jobs table as the authoritative schedule and the cache only as a disposable wake-up/routing hint. Correctness must survive cache eviction, delayed writes, duplicate deliveries, and worker crashes.

## Recommended design

- Durable row: jobs(id, due_at, revision, lease_epoch, status, …) with an index supporting due-job scans.
- Cache key per shard/bucket, e.g. next_due:{queue}:{partition}; value includes at least (min_due_at, generation/revision metadata).
- On creating or moving a runnable job earlier, write the durable change transactionally, then upsert the cache only toward an earlier time:sqlINSERT INTO routing_hints (bucket, due_at) VALUES ($bucket, $new_due) ON CONFLICT (bucket) DO UPDATE SET due_at = LEAST(routing_hints.due_at, EXCLUDED.due_at);PostgreSQL’s INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE provides an atomic insert-or-update outcome under concurrency; an update WHERE predicate is evaluated after identifying and locking the conflicting row.
```
INSERT INTO routing_hints (bucket, due_at) VALUES ($bucket, $new_due) ON CONFLICT (bucket) DO UPDATE SET due_at = LEAST(routing_hints.due_at, EXCLUDED.due_at);
```
Do not require every postponement, completion, cancellation, or lease renewal to perfectly edit the cache. Those are optimizations, not correctness operations.

## Conditional removal

Never delete a hint merely because a worker handled an old job. Delete/replace only conditionally, using a durable monotonic revision or lease epoch captured when the hint/work was observed:
```
DELETE FROM routing_hints WHERE bucket = $bucket AND revision = $observed_revision;
```
Or perform the equivalent atomic compare-and-delete in Redis/DynamoDB/etc. AWS documents the same optimistic-locking shape: update/delete succeeds only when the stored version matches the version previously read; a mismatch means refresh and retry.
A lease epoch should increase every time ownership is granted. A stale worker whose lease expired must not clear a hint created by the new owner.

## Races to expect

- Earlier schedule vs stale cleanup. A worker reads hint revision 7. Another transaction schedules an earlier job and publishes revision 8. The worker’s unconditional delete loses the wake-up; revision-conditional deletion fails instead, preserving revision 8.
- Two earlier writers. Writers propose 10:00 and 09:00 concurrently. LEAST converges to 09:00; never use last-writer-wins for the due time.
- Cache write loss after SQL commit. The job exists durably but no hint appears. Workers must periodically scan SQL for due_at <= now() and rebuild bucket minima. Also run a reconciler that scans active jobs, reconstructs hints, and tolerates duplicate publications.
- Duplicate execution/expired lease. Claim jobs in SQL with an atomic state/epoch predicate; make handlers idempotent. PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED re-evaluates a row’s WHERE condition after waiting on a concurrent updater, and ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE follows similar behavior. SKIP LOCKED is appropriate for queue-like multi-consumer claiming, but it intentionally presents an inconsistent view—so it is not a substitute for reconciliation.

## Primitive vs policy

PostgreSQL supplies atomic upserts, row locking, transactions, and conditional predicates—not “disposable cache correctness.” AWS supplies version-conditional writes as an optimistic-concurrency primitive, while its queue guidance explicitly assumes duplicates and recommends idempotent processing. The source-of-truth rule, minimum-only hint invariant, epochs, periodic durable scans, and cache rebuild loop are your application protocol.

Sources:
1. [postgresql](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html)
